title: The Phone Call and the Photograph
text:
In 1977 Mark Snyder, Elizabeth Tanke and Ellen Berscheid of the University of Minnesota asked pairs of male and female students, who had never met, to get acquainted in a ten-minute phone conversation. Before the call, each man was handed a snapshot that he believed showed his partner. In fact the photo was of someone else, chosen to be either very attractive or quite unattractive. The women did not know about any photo.

Before talking, the men who expected an attractive partner predicted she would be sociable, poised, humorous and socially adept, while those who expected an unattractive partner predicted the opposite. Then the conversations were recorded.

Independent judges later listened only to the women's half of each conversation, knowing nothing about the photographs. They rated the women whose partners believed they were attractive as more friendly, likable and sociable, and as enjoying themselves more. The men who thought they were talking with a beauty had been warmer and more engaging, and the women had responded in kind. The men's belief had created the very behavior it expected. The researchers called it a self-fulfilling stereotype: our expectations of people can draw out of them the behavior that seems to confirm those expectations.
lesson: How you expect someone to be shapes how you treat them, and they respond in kind. Approach people expecting the best, and you will often see it.
people: Mark Snyder, Elizabeth Tanke, Ellen Berscheid
source: Snyder, M., Tanke, E. D., and Berscheid, E. (1977). Social perception and interpersonal behavior: On the self-fulfilling nature of social stereotypes. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 35(9), 656-666.
